client: Hey Luna, I’ve been really anxious lately about the family reunion next month. My cousin always finds a way to criticize my career choices in front of everyone, and it makes me feel so embarrassed and inadequate. I don’t know if talking about it will really help, but I thought I’d bring it up.
therapist: I can understand how that situation with your cousin might be causing a lot of anxiety and discomfort. It’s really brave of you to share this, and it’s completely normal to feel embarrassed and inadequate in those moments. Have you had any thoughts about what might help you feel more prepared or confident going into the reunion?

client: I’ve thought about maybe avoiding him as much as possible, but I know that’s not really a solution. I just don’t want to feel so vulnerable and exposed. It’s hard because I can’t control what he says, and it always seems to catch me off guard.
therapist: It makes sense that you’d consider avoiding him, but I can see how that might not feel like a long-term solution. It’s totally understandable to feel vulnerable and exposed, especially when criticism feels unpredictable. Have you considered what it might look like to set some mental boundaries or prepare some responses that could help you feel more in control during these interactions?

client: I appreciate the idea of setting mental boundaries, but I’m not sure how to do that in the moment. It feels like I freeze up and can’t think of anything to say. Preparing responses sounds good, but I worry it might come off as defensive or make things worse.
therapist: It’s completely normal to feel like you freeze up in those moments; it’s a common reaction to stress and can be really challenging. Preparing responses doesn’t have to be about being defensive; it can be more about empowering yourself to stay calm and assertive. What do you think might help you feel more grounded and less reactive when you’re around your cousin? Maybe there’s a phrase or a mindset that could help you stay centered?

client: I like the idea of staying calm and assertive, but it’s hard to imagine myself doing that in the moment. Maybe if I had a simple phrase to remind myself that his opinions don’t define me, it could help. But I’m still worried that I’ll end up feeling embarrassed no matter what I do.
therapist: It’s really insightful of you to recognize that a simple phrase could help you stay grounded. Finding a phrase that resonates with you can be a powerful tool. What about something like, "His opinions are just that—opinions. They don’t define my value or my choices"? It might also be helpful to practice this phrase or a similar one in a safe environment to build your confidence. How do you think you could make this phrase a part of your preparation for the reunion?

client: I like the phrase, "His opinions are just that—opinions. They don’t define my value or my choices." It feels like something I can really stand behind. But I’m still nervous about actually using it in the moment. I guess I could try practicing it a few times before the reunion, but I’m not sure how much it will help when the real situation is so intense.
therapist: It’s great to hear that the phrase resonates with you, and practicing it beforehand is a good step. It’s normal to feel nervous about using it in a real, intense situation. Have you thought about also practicing some deep breathing or grounding techniques to help you stay calm and centered when you’re feeling anxious? This could make it easier to recall and use your phrase when you need it most.

client: I think deep breathing and grounding techniques could be helpful, but I’m not sure I’ll remember to do them in the heat of the moment. It’s hard to think clearly when I’m feeling so anxious. I’ll try practicing them, but I’m still skeptical about how much they’ll actually help when I’m face-to-face with my cousin.
therapist: It’s totally understandable to feel skeptical, especially when anxiety can make it hard to think clearly. Practicing these techniques regularly can help them become more automatic over time, even in stressful situations. What do you think might help you feel more confident in using these tools, even if just a little, during the reunion? Maybe there’s a small step you can take to make it feel more manageable?

client: I think if I can practice the deep breathing and grounding techniques a few times each day leading up to the reunion, it might help a little. It’s still a big ask, but I can try to make it a small part of my routine. I’m just hoping it will give me a bit more control when I’m around my cousin.
therapist: That’s a really practical and manageable plan, and I’m glad you’re willing to give it a try. Starting small and integrating these techniques into your daily routine can make a big difference. It’s okay to approach this with a mix of hope and skepticism; even a small increase in control can be a significant step forward. How do you think you’ll know if the techniques are helping, even in subtle ways, as you go through the reunion?

client: I think I’ll know if the techniques are helping if I can stay a bit more calm and composed when my cousin starts talking. Even if I don’t manage to say anything assertive, just not feeling as overwhelmed or embarrassed would be a win. It’s a small goal, but it feels achievable.
therapist: That’s a fantastic goal, and it’s great that you’ve identified what success might look like for you. Staying calm and composed, even if you don’t say anything assertive, is a significant achievement. It’s all about making progress in a way that feels manageable and realistic. How do you think you might reflect on your experience after the reunion to see if you’ve made any steps toward your goal, no matter how small?

client: I think I’ll take some time to journal about my experience right after the reunion. Writing down how I felt and what I managed to do differently might help me see the progress, even if it’s just a small step. It’s hard to be objective in the moment, so having a way to reflect later could be really helpful.
therapist: Journaling is a wonderful way to gain clarity and reflect on your experience. It can help you see the progress you’ve made and the strengths you’ve used, even when it’s hard to recognize them in the moment. How do you think you might celebrate or acknowledge the small steps you take, no matter how subtle they might be, to keep yourself motivated and encouraged?

client: I like the idea of celebrating small steps, but it’s hard for me to feel like I’ve accomplished something when I’m so used to feeling like I fail. Maybe I could treat myself to something I enjoy, like a favorite snack or a relaxing activity, after the reunion. It might help me see that even small efforts are worth acknowledging.
therapist: That’s a really thoughtful way to approach it, and treating yourself to something you enjoy is a great way to acknowledge your efforts. Recognizing and rewarding your small steps can help build a more positive mindset over time. How do you think you might remind yourself to celebrate these moments, even when the urge to dismiss them is strong? Maybe there’s a way to make it a part of your routine or a mental note you can make?
